title: Choose the landing page's world
question: The roll landed on The Edit Bay. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Edit Bay
options.lineage: nonlinear editor timelines (Premiere, Resolve) at 2 a.m.
options.thesis: The whole page is an edit timeline: scroll is the playhead, and you watch a long video get cut into Shorts and posted.
options.viewport: A full-width timeline. Track V1 holds one long 16:9 source; as the playhead moves, razor cuts lift 9:16 clips onto track V2 with burned captions, and a POST track drops markers 10:00 apart. Headline and Sign up sit in the program-monitor panel above.
options.risk: Needs real motion craft; a static picture of a timeline reads as a screenshot.

raised.raise: Clip states (queued, uploading, posted, flagged) are painted onto the clips on the track, never shown as separate badges.
Post markers wake one after another in a timed sequence, so the 10-minute gap is something you see, not something you read.
Every heavy section has a fast version beside it: the three-command quick start next to the full setup.
The playhead is a real scroll-driven instrument, built once and committed to, not a decorative picture.

options.label: The Cutting Room
options.lineage: film editors' cutting rooms, contact sheets and grease pencil
options.thesis: A strip of celluloid gets sliced into vertical frames, marked up in grease pencil and taped to a contact sheet.
options.viewport: A 16:9 film strip runs across a light table; a grease-pencil box frames a 9:16 window on it, and the headline is hand-marked beside the cut.
options.risk: Celluloid nostalgia can read as a film school site rather than a dev tool.

options.label: Swiss Poster Wall
options.thesis: Each pipeline step is one poster on a single strict grid; the wall reads as one calm machine.
options.viewport: Five posters in a row (Download, Transcribe, Pick, Render, Post), each with one geometric motif and a giant step number.
options.case: Holds product clarity well; developers identify with it less than with an editor or a terminal.
options.risk: Cool and correct can read as a design agency, not a tool.

options.label: Phosphor Terminal
options.thesis: The page is the worker's own log: the real progress messages scroll by as a video becomes posted Shorts.
options.viewport: A full-screen transcript: $ pnpm dev, then Downloading video..., Creating clip 3/8..., Posted clip 1 at 16:40.
options.case: Developers know it by heart; showing vertical video output inside a terminal is weaker on clarity.
options.risk: Terminal pages are common on dev-tool sites, so it can look familiar.

options.label: Living Skin
options.thesis: The surface changes pattern to signal state.
options.viewport: A living textile field behind the headline.
options.case: Fuses poorly: nothing about it says video, Shorts or setup.
options.kept: State drawn directly on the object.

options.label: Versailles Vistas
options.viewport: An axial vista down the page.
options.case: Fuses poorly: grandeur fights a developer tool.

options.label: Wildstyle Blackbook
options.thesis: Interlocked letterforms with a fast throw-up aside.
options.viewport: The name as an interlocked piece.
options.case: Fuses poorly: setup steps need legibility above all.
options.kept: A fast version beside the full one.

options.label: Shader Portal
options.thesis: A living shader field with thin type over it.
options.viewport: One hero word over moving pixels.
options.case: Fuses poorly: says nothing specific about clipping or posting.
options.kept: Total commitment to one real technique.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A classic open-source dev-tool landing page, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Headline, GitHub and Sign up buttons, a big app screenshot, then features and a copyable quick start.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other open-source tool by design.
